cards.title: Position on a Two-Axis Map, Not on Competitors' Claims
cards.summary: Use a simple XY grid of customer-relevant attributes to find an uncrowded positioning quadrant for your store or product line.
cards.use_when: Choosing brand positioning, category angle, or PDP messaging when your store sells in a crowded category (snacks, supplements, apparel, tools) and you need a defensible reason to be chosen.
steps: List all alternatives your customer could consider (not just direct competitors): other brands, other store types, marketplaces, DIY, doing nothing.

Pick two axes that customers actually care about, e.g. price vs. status, convenience vs. security, purity vs. indulgence, speed vs. sustainability. The source offers a long menu: performance, ingredients, maintenance cost, safety, edginess, distribution, trendiness, privacy, professionalism, elitism.
Plot every alternative on the grid. If several cluster in the same spot, that quadrant is crowded and hard to win without a big ad budget.
Choose a spot on an edge where few offerings sit, and make sure you can actually deliver it operationally (spec, sourcing, service, returns).
Rewrite your homepage, product page and ad copy around that single claim. Choose your extremes and you choose your market, and vice versa.
Re-run the exercise with different axes periodically; the same category can be re-mapped many ways.
caveats: Positioning claims only work if they are true and consistently delivered; a claim you cannot keep becomes a commodity in the making.
Picking a popular axis usually means a crowded quadrant where customers default to doing nothing or buying on price.

cards.title: Market to the Buyer, Not the End User
cards.summary: Dog food is bought by owners, not dogs — identify the person who actually makes the purchase decision and their emotional payoff.
cards.use_when: Product development, packaging or PDP copy for any store where the buyer differs from the user (pet products, kids' goods, gifts, B2B tools bought by a manager).
steps: Identify who clicks 'buy' and who lives with the product. They may have completely different criteria.
List the buyer's inputs and emotions (status, generosity, care, guilt, convenience), not just the user's functional requirements.
Check whether your feature roadmap and copy are optimized for the user's experience or the buyer's feeling. 'Performance and appeal' are usually disconnected.
Reframe value propositions around what the buyer gets: the satisfaction of good care, the status of a luxury good, the generosity of sharing.
Keep functional quality as table stakes; the emotional layer is what drives the choice between near-identical products.
caveats: This is a reasoning framework from a marketing book, not a tested ecommerce benchmark; validate with your own buyer interviews or returns/refund data.

cards.title: Serve Early Adopters Differently From the Main Market
cards.summary: Neophiliacs want new, interesting and unfinished; the mainstream wants reliable and familiar — these need separate products, copy and channels.
cards.use_when: Deciding which SKUs or editions to launch first, how to sequence drops, and whether to write clever experimental copy or reassuring mainstream copy.
steps: Classify the product's current stage: is it built for discovery-seekers or for people who want the world to stay the same?
For early adopters, emphasize novelty, insider status, and 'this might not work' tension. They forgive missteps during the thrill of discovery and brag about finds.
For the mainstream, emphasize reliability, safety, and reduced risk. Laggards want things not to change.
Don't expect early adopters to stay loyal once the newness fades; plan the transition to a broader audience and repeat purchase before the initial tribe loses interest.
Write separate landing pages, ad creative and email flows for the two groups rather than one averaged message.
The magic question before any launch or campaign: who's it for?
caveats: Early adopters are described as forgiving early and unforgiving later; 'you can't be perfect in the eyes of an early adopter, the best you can do is be interesting' is the source's claim, not a universal law.
cards.source_name: This Is Marketing_ You Can’t Be Seen Until You Learn to Se (1).docx

cards.title: Position as a Service: A Generous Signal Flare, Not a USP
cards.summary: Replace a self-serving unique selling proposition with a clear signal that helps the people looking for you find you.
cards.use_when: Writing your brand's core promise for the homepage hero, About page or ad hook when the current message is a generic superiority claim.
steps: Start from an audience worth serving and their needs, wants and dreams; build the offering for them rather than inventing a claim to fill a market hole.
Choose what to stand for and what to be against — 'we're this, not that' — and repeat it across every touchpoint.
Be generous with the claim: it should exist as a service to the customer, not as a boast about you.
Make the claim concrete enough to act on operationally, including which customers you'll decline or which requests you won't take.
Use the same signal in ads, packaging, PDP headline and support scripts so the promise is recognised, not just asserted.
caveats: Old positioning practice (invent a claim to fill an empty spot) is described as not holding up in a hyper-competitive market; claims must be true and continually doubled down on in all actions.
cards.source_name: This Is Marketing_ You Can’t Be Seen Until You Learn to Se (1).docx

cards.title: Micro-Tribes: Sell Uniqueness and Belonging, Not Consensus
cards.summary: Outlier psychology shows people are drawn to small, distinct groups — a niche signal can beat a broadly appealing one.
cards.use_when: Community building, loyalty programs, or positioning a niche store or limited drop against a mass-market competitor.
steps: Identify the small, outspoken group your product already appeals to and where they gather (forums, Discords, subreddits, local scenes).
Design the offer so belonging is visible: shared identifiers, member-only products, limited runs, insider language.
Give members something to brag about — a discovery or knowledge that outsiders don't have.
Prefer depth in the micro-tribe over reaching a broad indifferent audience; the source's study of conspiracy believers found stronger engagement when told only 19% shared the belief than 81%.
Translate that into ecommerce: edition sizes, member pricing, community-only drops, and visible badges of belonging rather than mass discounting.
caveats: The underlying study concerns conspiracy theorists, not shoppers; the transferable point is about uniqueness-seeking behaviour, and should be tested with your own customers.
cards.source_name: This Is Marketing_ You Can’t Be Seen Until You Learn to Se (1).docx

cards.title: Run the 'It's a Test' Loop Instead of Betting on a Miracle
cards.summary: Shipping a real offer to real early adopters is faster and more honest than waiting for a hype-driven hit.
cards.use_when: Launching a new product, bundle or landing page when you're tempted to perfect it before exposing it to the market.
steps: Make an assertion about what a specific group wants and turn it into a concrete promise and offer.
Because prototypes and limited runs are now cheap, ship a real test — a small batch, a pre-order, a single landing page — rather than a polished plan for later.
Expose it to curious, dissatisfied or bored people, who are the only ones who will pay attention.
Expect to be wrong most of the time; treat wrongness as the cost of finding the edge, not a reason to stop.
Use the findings to choose new extremes and repeat, rather than concluding the idea itself was bad.
Design being tested into normal operations: always be seeking, connecting, solving, asserting and testing.
caveats: The source presents this as a heuristic, not a numeric success rate; 'most of the time you'll be wrong' is its opinion, not a measured benchmark.
cards.source_name: This Is Marketing_ You Can’t Be Seen Until You Learn to Se (1).docx

cards.title: Start From the Problem and the Change, Not the Product
cards.summary: Effective offers begin with a group to serve, a problem they want solved, and the change they want to make.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to build, stock or promote next; writing the top of a landing page; evaluating whether a new SKU has a real reason to exist.
steps: Write down the group you seek to serve, the problem they seek to solve, and the change they seek to make before listing product features.
Frame the change emotionally, not tactically: a new emotional state is what's being purchased, not the widget.
Check whether the claim serves the customer's interest or only makes you look clever; commodity alternatives have no claim at all.
Ask whether the change is one the customer already wants or one you'd have to argue them into.
Turn this into an offer statement and test it against your product page headline and first screen.
caveats: Quality and meeting specification remain required but are no longer sufficient — this framework assumes you can already deliver reliably.
cards.source_name: This Is Marketing_ You Can’t Be Seen Until You Learn to Se (1).docx

cards.title: Sell the Emotional State, Not the Object
cards.summary: People buy feelings, status and connection; identify the feeling before designing the product.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, choosing product photography or naming a new line, especially for non-essential goods.
steps: For each product, list plausible feelings the buyer is chasing (confidence, belonging, nostalgia, status, peace of mind, being seen).
Pick the one or two feelings your audience is genuinely seeking rather than the most obvious functional benefit.
Design the product presentation — images, copy, bundle, unboxing, return policy — to deliver that feeling.
Example from the source: a first car for a teenager is a status shift for the teen and a change in control for the parent; the marketing must serve both emotional shifts.
Check that the functional claims support the emotional promise rather than contradicting it.
caveats: The source argues people are bad at inventing new ways to satisfy their wants and often default to familiar solutions; a new emotional angle needs to connect to an existing want.
cards.source_name: This Is Marketing_ You Can’t Be Seen Until You Learn to Se (1).docx

cards.title: Find the Bear: Diagnose Non-Purchase as Fear
cards.summary: When customers don't behave as expected, look for fear blocking the purchase before blaming the offer's obvious features.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing low conversion, abandoned carts, low retention or poor response to a new offer.
steps: For each step of the funnel, ask what the customer is afraid of: being cheated, being judged, wasting money, being seen with the wrong thing.
Look at friction that signals risk: unclear returns, hidden shipping cost, unfamiliar payment, no social proof, aggressive urgency copy.
Check whether your own anxiety-driven copy is amplifying their fear rather than answering it.
Replace fear with concrete reassurance where the fear is real, and with a status or belonging cue where the fear is social.
Test the change; do not assume that lower price is the answer to a fear-based problem.
caveats: This is a diagnostic heuristic from the source; it doesn't replace funnel data, session recordings or customer interviews.
cards.source_name: This Is Marketing_ You Can’t Be Seen Until You Learn to Se (1).docx

cards.title: Design Remarkability Into the Product Itself
cards.summary: Products that work better when friends use them together grow by themselves; add-on marketing can't do that job.
cards.use_when: Designing referral mechanics, gifting options, multiplayer features, or shared/subscription plans in a store.
steps: Ask of any product or feature: does it work better, or feel better, if my customer's friend also has it?
If not, consider adding a shared element: gifting, group buying, referral credit, a two-person bundle, or community-generated content.

Model the network logic rather than assuming it: cost of adding users rises roughly linearly, while value is said to rise much faster — the source cites Metcalfe's Law and the fax machine/Ethernet examples.
Make the spread visible and easy so that word of mouth is the growth engine rather than paid reach alone.
Watch whether your best customers actually recruit; if not, the design isn't doing the work yet.
caveats: Network effects do not apply to every category; the source generalizes from fax machines and Ethernet. Verify before restructuring a physical-goods store around them.
cards.source_name: This Is Marketing_ You Can’t Be Seen Until You Learn to Se (1).docx

cards.title: Build Customer Traction in the Small Before Chasing Scale
cards.summary: Check daily usage, requests for improvement and peer insistence before believing a growth plan will work.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a new product line, store concept, or marketing budget increase — deciding whether to scale or fix the core first.
steps: Ask how many people outside your company use the product every day, and how often they send improvement suggestions.
Ask how many are actively insisting that friends and colleagues use it right now.
Ask whether they'd miss it if it were gone, and whether they come back repeatedly bringing new customers.
If you can't succeed in the small, the source argues, there is little reason to believe you'll succeed in the large.
Fix retention and organic recommendation before raising acquisition spend; expensive failure is the usual outcome of the 'miracle' approach.
caveats: The source is addressing startups, restaurants and market stalls; adapt the metrics (repeat purchase rate, referral rate, request volume) to your store rather than copying the wording.
cards.source_name: This Is Marketing_ You Can’t Be Seen Until You Learn to Se (1).docx

cards.title: Use the Thousand True Fans Sizing Rule for Niche Offers
cards.summary: A small number of superfans who buy nearly everything can sustain a business, so niche depth may beat mass reach.
cards.use_when: Sizing a niche subscription, membership or creator-style product line and deciding whether to chase a broad market instead.
steps: Define a true fan for your store: buys nearly every drop, pays full price, waits for restocks, and brings others.
Estimate how many such customers exist and what each is worth across a year, including repeat purchases.
Compare that against the cost of competing for low-loyalty broad-market buyers.
Design the offer so superfans want everything you make — collectible editions, member perks, advance access, a consistent story.
Use the source's rule of thumb (Kevin Kelly's 1000 true fans) as a sizing heuristic: 1,000 people who buy your next release the day it launches can support a modest living.
caveats: The thousand-fan figure is a source-specific rule of thumb about living income for independent creators, not a proven ecommerce benchmark; substitute your own unit economics.
cards.source_name: This Is Marketing_ You Can’t Be Seen Until You Learn to Se (1).docx

cards.title: Scrapbook Proven Elements Instead of Inventing From Scratch
cards.summary: Improve conversion and design faster by breaking down trusted references into their parts and recombining them.
cards.use_when: Building a landing page, email campaign or new product listing when time is limited and you need a credible starting point.
steps: Collect references your audience already trusts and responds to: competitor pages, category leaders, respected non-competitor experiences.
Break each down into indivisible elements — typefaces, pricing display, offer structure, imagery style, interface patterns.
Identify the beacons (your chosen extremes) that matter to you and your audience, and discard the rest.
Recombine the pieces into a new thing rather than copying a whole design.
Test the rebuilt page against incumbents; scrapbooking is an efficiency play, not a guarantee of originality or outperformance.
caveats: Radical originality is described as low-ROI and exhausting; this method trades distinctiveness for speed and reuse.
Avoid drifting into a generic look by keeping the positioning extremes explicit.
cards.source_name: This Is Marketing_ You Can’t Be Seen Until You Learn to Se (1).docx

cards.title: Price With the Ten-Times Question
cards.summary: Ask what would justify charging ten times more — the answer must be a different story and different scarcity, not more of the same.
cards.use_when: Pricing a premium tier, a luxury bundle, a membership, or a high-end physical product.
steps: Ask directly: what would make this worth ten times its current price?
Reject 'more of the same' answers: more words, a larger portion, or a louder stereo doesn't multiply willingness to pay.
Look for a different extreme, a different story, or a different type of scarcity — access, status, curation, exclusivity, relationship, or transformation.

Check whether your highest-priced competitors are priced by features or by story; the source's example is an ice cream cone at a near-Ottawa resort that could rationally be priced at peak margin but is deliberately kept cheap as a beacon and engagement device.
Decide deliberately whether this SKU is a profit centre or a beacon; don't let a spreadsheet turn a strategic loss-leader into a price increase that kills its job.
caveats: The resort and supermarket examples are anecdotes illustrating the irrational side of pricing, not evidence that raising prices always works.
cards.source_name: This Is Marketing_ You Can’t Be Seen Until You Learn to Se (1).docx

cards.title: Add an Offline or Human Element Online Retail Can't Copy
cards.summary: A physical or experiential differentiator lets a retailer compete with cheaper online sellers without a price war.
cards.use_when: Merchandising and positioning a physical store, showroom, pop-up, or local pickup experience against Amazon and other online retailers.
steps: Identify what an online-only seller structurally cannot provide: a place to meet, a third place, coffee, expertise, try-on, same-day pickup, repair.
Make that element central rather than incidental — the source describes Trident Booksellers as a coffee shop that sells books, where the books are a souvenir of a personal connection.
Reframe merchandise in support of the experience rather than the other way round.
Communicate the human element on the store's pages and signage; don't bury it as a footnote.
Consider the source's suggested tagline pattern: '. . . and we serve coffee' — a concrete, non-generic promise that location-based competitors can't copy.
caveats: This applies to retailers with a physical presence; pure online operators need an equivalent human element (expert advice, community, live events) to get the same effect.
cards.source_name: This Is Marketing_ You Can’t Be Seen Until You Learn to Se (1).docx

cards.title: Perform Emotional Labor Instead of Striving for Authenticity
cards.summary: In the marketplace, professional service and empathy beat raw authenticity; present the best version of the work, not every feeling.
cards.use_when: Customer service scripting, brand voice, founder-led content, UGC and support replies where the founder's mood and the brand's message conflict.
steps: Accept that marketplace 'authenticity' is a myth: the barista's smile and James Brown's stage collapse are performance, repeated every night.
Treat emotional labor as the job: showing up with empathy for what the customer wants, even when you don't feel like it.
Guard against the 'authentic jerk' problem — if the real you is selfish, keep it out of the storefront.
Endorse the work with the human phrase the source offers: 'Here, I made this' — take responsibility as a person, not a faceless corporation speaking in the second person.
Make the work personal rather than personalized: a signature, a named founder, a real reply, not automated intimacy.
caveats: The source argues authenticity is a dangerous myth and that professionals play roles; this is a strong opinion, and some categories and creator brands legitimately benefit from raw disclosure.
cards.source_name: This Is Marketing_ You Can’t Be Seen Until You Learn to Se (1).docx

cards.title: Assert the Customer's Beliefs Before Choosing Channels
cards.summary: Research should surface what the audience believes and wants, then you assert a promise, not ask them to invent the product.
cards.use_when: Writing briefs for acquisition creative, ad hooks, or a pre-launch validation plan.
steps: Start from the shared basket of dreams and desires the source lists: adventure, affection, belonging, community, control, creativity, delight, freedom, friendship, good looks, health, learning, luxury, nostalgia, peace of mind, power, reassurance, reliability, respect, romance, safety, security, sex, strength, sympathy, tension.
Write assertions about what your audience wants, what is on their mind when they wake up, and what they remember at the end of the day.
Do not expect customers to invent new solutions: ask them and you mostly get familiar answers and conservative preferences.
Accept that wants and needs get confused — almost everything beyond air, water, health and shelter is a want, treated by the buyer as a need.
Then build the promise and the creative, and test whether people see what you see and take action.
caveats: The source warns customers are bad at inventing breakthrough solutions; treat survey answers as constraints, not blueprints.
cards.source_name: This Is Marketing_ You Can’t Be Seen Until You Learn to Se (1).docx

cards.title: Replace 'You Can Choose Anyone, and We're Anyone' with an Edge
cards.summary: Functional parity is table stakes; a true and generous edge is what makes a store the clear and obvious choice.
cards.use_when: Rewriting an undifferentiated homepage or category page that competes only on price.
steps: Audit your messaging: if it could be swapped onto a competitor's site unchanged, you have a commodity problem.

Identify the edge only you can claim authentically — the source's example is a music teacher claiming 'I'm serious, my students are serious, this is about rigor' plus 'my students win competitions', which requires expelling students who aren't serious.
Accept the operational consequences: a sharp positioning means turning away the customers it isn't for.
A neighbouring competitor can occupy a completely different position (whole-student, non-competitive, connection-led) — you aren't competing, you're on the same board.
Choose the popular, broad axes or you'll land in a crowded quadrant where customers, unsure, do nothing.
caveats: The source attributes this 'commodity suckout' risk partly to price transparency: your customers now often know more about your competitors than you do.
